title: Review of Data, Models, and Decisions on GraduateTutor.com (unsigned page of a tutoring company, linked by the publisher)
contribution: Unsigned tutoring-company review (reviewer's voice, weak evidence; about 2014, inferred): praises DMD's decision-first, unified statistics-plus-OR/MS design and lists dropped topics, asking whether students lose depth. Its topic list equals the ten chapter titles of the 2000 edition (B015 pp. 1-5); its omissions agree with those titles except 'inferences' (Ch. 4 has confidence intervals and two-sample comparisons, B015 p. 2); the third edition it expected is not on his 2017 or 2026 book pages (B008 pp. 1-2). The book's Dynamic Ideas page links it (B014 p. 1); nothing in it is Bertsimas's voice (p. 1).
problem_entry: {DA AP; teaching} Reviewer's framing: MBA programmes teach statistics and operations research in two courses, often from two departments, and textbooks serve them separately; the book is 'unique' in combining business statistics and OR/MS in one book, is 'primarily used by first year MBA students' and puts decision making first. The page is written by a company that sells tutoring for the book (p. 1).
key_idea: Reviewer's reading of the design, five 'unique' features: decision making as the focus (frameworks, not standard topics); one book for statistics and OR/MS; topics selected from decision making outward ('an optimal mix' for 'a tight MBA semester'); suitable for beginners; decision trees first, not in the middle or at the end. Topic list, introduced as the second edition's: ten items from decision analysis to 'Integration in the art of decision modeling' (p. 1). Cross-check, title level: the ten items are the 2000 edition's chapter titles in order (B015 pp. 1-5); Ch. 1 opens with a decision-tree model and its section 1.4 is 'The Need for a Systematic Theory of Probability' (B015 p. 1), so the tree motivates the probability that follows [inferred]; the second edition's page keeps simulation in Ch. 5, optimization in Chs. 7-9 and the capstone in Ch. 10 (B014 p. 1), so the chapter order probably did not change [inferred].
assumptions: D3 read for a review (the reviewer's evidence base): no method of review stated, no chapter quoted; the only remark below title level is that Ch. 1 'leaves out the expected value of perfect information'. Edition facts (first edition 2000, South-Western College Pub./Thomson Learning, 'seems to have been'; second edition Dynamic Ideas 2004; 'updated only once'; a third edition expected) and a CD with Crystal Ball and Excel files (p. 1). Relayed: MIT OCW's 15.060 course description, quoted in full, not checked (its wording differs from the Fall 2002 archive description held for S797; a guessed Fall 2007 OCW URL returned 404 on 2026-10-29). Second-hand author paragraphs: Bertsimas's paper topics mirror his old archive folders (01 §1.2, inferred) and his two motivations for robust optimization follow the wording of his old Research page (https://www.mit.edu/~dbertsim/research.html, Last-Modified 2017-09-08, checked 2026-10-29); Freund is credited with HBS's quantitative methods curriculum (not checked). Nothing of Bertsimas's voice (p. 1).
experiments: n/a for computation. Adoption relayed, unverified: 'the prescribed text book for the MIT Sloan MBA program introductory course of the same title'; ten named US universities and, abroad, the American University of Afghanistan, City University of Hong Kong, the National University of Singapore and 'other universities in China'; OCW archives of Fall 2002 and Fall 2007 (p. 1). Cross-check: the authors' page claims classroom pre-testing (a different claim) at eight schools plus several overseas; the two lists share only MIT (B014 p. 1).
positioning: Yardsticks: 'most text books' (standard-topic coverage; decision trees in the middle or at the end), the two-course, two-department MBA model, and 'introductory statistics text books' and 'introductory operations modeling text books' for what is missing; no textbook, reviewer or author named, nothing cited (p. 1). Features 1-2 restate the authors' own page (a departure from methodology-led textbooks; 'Unified Treatment of Quantitative Methods', B014 p. 1): agreement, not an independent test.
writing: Promotional page in the company's 'we': verdict and recommendation, five bulleted 'unique' features, adoption list and relayed OCW text, a tutoring pitch mid-page, editions, topic list, limitations, a depth question, software, author paragraphs (one 'my', as 'a finance tutor'), a sign-up close. Criticism is raised then defused ('Critics may opine' ... 'an optimal mix'; 'It is inevitable' ... 'a good job'); the one open criticism is a question about depth. Reading notes, not findings: loose course names ('15.071 – The Analytical Edge'; '5.072 – Queues: Theory and Applications') (p. 1).
limits_future: Reviewer's criticisms: Ch. 1 omits the expected value of perfect information; 'Combining two courses into one creates limitations': missing statistics topics (descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, 'inferences and analysis of variance', the expected value of perfect information) and operations-modelling topics (discriminant analysis, forecasting, queueing); students might be better off with more depth in each subject separately; software on a CD and one revision since 2000, with a third edition expected (p. 1). Cross-checks, title level, 2000 edition: none of these topics has a section title (B015 pp. 1-5), but Ch. 4 has confidence intervals (4.3, 4.5, 4.6), 4.7 Experimental Design and two-sample comparisons (4.8, 4.9) (B015 p. 2), so 'inferences' holds only in a narrow sense; regression is taught for prediction (6.1-6.2 and two prediction cases, B015 pp. 3-5), with no time-series forecasting title. The authors' page speaks to depth with another aim: retained fundamental concepts and concise coverage (B014 p. 1, paraphrase). No third edition on his 2017 or 2026 book pages (B008 pp. 1-2). Card-writer's note [inferred]: queueing, his own SD field, has no title in the MBA text. Route to 05-peer-critique.md (no entry for this book yet) as the voice of an unsigned commercial reviewer.

method_links.note: Peer view, weak (unsigned, commercial), teaching level: an outside reader finds the book decision-first in aim, topic selection and order (frameworks for decision making; decision trees first). That is the teaching form of Research Taste mark 4 and the opposite of warning sign 6 and the anti-pattern 'Methods-first teaching' [02 T9]. It restates the authors' claims (B014 p. 1) rather than testing them; only the order can be checked, at title level (B015 p. 1).

Peer view, unverified: the course -> book stage seen from outside. The book is reported as the prescribed text of the same-titled MIT Sloan core course, with OCW archives and adoption at named schools; none of this was checked, and his own account of the step is the 2014 oral history (01 §1.9). Revised once (2000 -> 2004); no third edition on his 2017 or 2026 book pages (B008 pp. 1-2), so for this book step 5 ends in 2004 as far as those pages show.

Peer view, weak: the first critique on record of his DA teaching text (05-peer-critique.md has none). One course and one text in place of two subject courses drop standard topics and, the reviewer asks, perhaps depth. The omissions agree with the 2000 contents at title level except 'inferences' (B015 pp. 1-5). Route to 05 in the reviewer's voice, as an unsigned page.

The Remaining-gaps line stays true for S128: this card adds an outside reading and a topic list equal to the first edition's chapter titles, not the book's body; its one remark on content (no expected value of perfect information in Ch. 1) is unverified. In the disclaimer's coverage, count B016 as a review read, not as the book read. It supports no Stated line and nothing in the Domain Map's Voice column; a reception line must call it an unsigned GraduateTutor.com page.

transferable: When one course or text unifies two subjects around decisions, name in the preface the standard topics it drops and where to find them: this reviewer had to infer the omissions and asked whether depth suffered (p. 1), while the authors' page states the unification and its concision but names no omission (B014 p. 1).

Order a methods course by the decision: open with a decision model (here a decision tree) and let it motivate the tools that follow; the reviewer singles out this order as unusual (p. 1), and the first edition's contents follow it (B015 p. 1, title level).
coauthors: none (unsigned review by GraduateTutor.com, a tutoring company; not a Bertsimas work); the book reviewed is by Dimitris Bertsimas and Robert M. Freund

quotes.text: Unlike most text books, the objective is not to cover standard topics in statistics and operations research but to provide students frameworks for decision making.
One wonders, however, if students would be better off having more depth in statistics and operations management separately.
